tagline: Farmland, Satus Pass and a highway above the Columbia River
intro: The Yakama Scenic Byway climbs from the Yakima Valley’s farmland into the hills leading to Satus Pass, then continues toward the Columbia River. Scenic Washington presents the route through its farming towns, wilderness and Goldendale’s public observatory. Much of this drive through the Yakama people’s ancestral homeland lies within the Yakama Reservation.

Near its southern end, road building once meant experimenting with the climb out of the Columbia River country. In 1911, Samuel Hill and engineer Samuel C. Lancaster built Maryhill Loops Road, using horseshoe curves to keep grades low on Washington’s first asphalt road. US 97 acquired its federal number in 1926. The straighter US 97 bypassed that experimental road after World War II. At Maryhill, a ferry had crossed the Columbia since the early 1920s; the Sam Hill Memorial Bridge opened in 1962.

Follow the byway south from Union Gap on US 97 to Toppenish, then through Goldendale to SR 14 near Maryhill Museum. Fort Simcoe is a separate excursion west of Toppenish. South of Toppenish, the highway crosses the wildlife refuge before the climb toward Satus Pass; beyond the pass, forest gives way to the plateau at Goldendale and the descent through the Columbia Hills.

moments.title: Fort Simcoe
moments.text: Five original buildings remain at Fort Simcoe: the commander’s house, three captains’ houses and a blockhouse. Other buildings are recreations, a distinction that matters when looking across the former post. The Army built the fort in the late 1850s in an oak grove fed by natural springs and used it for three years. Its position lay on a Yakama route between the Yakima Valley and Columbia River fishing areas, allowing soldiers to monitor the tribe and its visitors. The preserved post is now a day-use heritage park on the Yakama Indian Reservation, with houses furnished in period style.

moments.title: Toppenish
moments.text: Toppenish’s first mural, “Clearing the Land,” was painted in 1989. More than 75 murals now cover its buildings, depicting regional scenes from 1840 to 1940. The town itself began in 1884 along the Northern Pacific Railway, within the Yakama Indian Reservation. Its 1911 depot later became the Northern Pacific Railway Museum. The railroad closed the depot in 1981; it remained boarded up for nearly ten years before a museum association formed in 1989. The painted scenes span a century of regional history; the depot gives that railway town’s past a building of its own.

moments.title: Goldendale
moments.text: Goldendale’s observatory began with a telescope looking for a home. Four amateur astronomers built the 24.5-inch reflector for Clark College in Vancouver, which paid for the materials. The college wanted a darker, clearer location than Vancouver, and a Goldendale diner owner and city council member suggested donating it to the town. The gift came with a condition: the community had to build an observatory. Dedicated in 1973, it was intended primarily for public science education. The observatory occupies a hill north of town, reached by a winding paved road through oak forest.
